How a mill pond holds the tide

The wheel[1] turns for as long as the pond holds water.

A second gate2 lets the tide out, and a third[note 3] is rarely used.

Two sources agree[4][5] that the pond lasts three hours.

It drains the water[6], and then it waits.

The pond[7]lasts until the gate opens.

The relation E = mc2 is not a footnote, and the 1st of May is a date.

An asterisk* and a dagger† mark the older notes in the margin.

See the pond section for the drawing, and the mill catalogue for the rest. [edit] stays, because those letters are a word.

Millers kept the gate shut for the hours the pond needed, and they opened it only when the wheel had somewhere to put the water. The stone turned at the speed the tide allowed, which is a slower speed than a river gives, and the flour came out the finer for it. Families who lived beside the pond learned the sound of the wheel the way other people learn a clock, and they slept when it stopped.

Notes

  1. ^ The pond held three hours of water.
  2. ↑ The second gate faces the sea.
